en: Theravāda Vinaya Bhikkhunīvibhaṅga Pācittiyakaṇḍa
Naggavagga 23.
The Training Rule on Sewing Robes.
At that time, the Buddha, the Blessed One, was staying at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.
Now at that time, a certain bhikkhunī had made a robe from a costly cloth, but it was poorly made and badly sewn.
The bhikkhunī Thullanandā said this to her:
"This robe-cloth of yours, noble lady, is indeed beautiful."
“But this robe-cloth is poorly sewn and badly stitched.
“I will re-sew it, noble lady; will you sew it?
“Yes, noble lady, I will sew it.”
Then that bhikkhunī, having unsewn that robe-cloth, gave it to the bhikkhunī Thullanandā.
The bhikkhunī Thullanandā,
thinking, "I will sew it, I will sew it," neither sewed it nor made any effort to have it sewn.
Then that bhikkhunī reported this matter to the bhikkhunīs.
Those bhikkhunīs who were few in desires... [as before]... were indignant, disparaged it, and complained, saying:
"How can the noble lady Thullanandā, having had a bhikkhunī’s robe opened out for her, neither sew it herself nor make an effort to have it sewn?"... [as before]...
“Is it true, monks, that the nun Thullanandā, having caused a nun’s robe to be unraveled, neither sews it herself nor makes an effort to have it sewn?
“It is true, Blessed One.
The Buddha, the Blessed One, rebuked her... [as before]...
“How, monks, could the bhikkhunī Thullanandā, having had a bhikkhunī’s robe unstitched, neither sew it herself nor make an effort to have it sewn?

This, monks, does not lead to the confidence of those without confidence … And so, monks, the bhikkhunīs should recite this training rule: “Whatever bhikkhunī, having had a bhikkhunī’s robe unstitched, neither sews it herself nor makes an effort to have it sewn, there is an offense of wrong-doing.”

“Whatever nun, having had a robe unsewn or having had it unsewn by another for a fellow nun, subsequently, while there is no obstacle, neither sews it herself nor makes an effort to have it sewn, except within four or five days, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
“Whatever nun” means whichever nun of such a kind... [and so forth].
"A bhikkhunī" ...
[as before] ... this is the kind of bhikkhunī intended in this context.
"Of a bhikkhunī":
"Of another nun.
"Robe" means any one of the six kinds of robes.
"Having sewn herself" means having sewn by herself.
"Having had sewn" means...
Having caused another [robe] to be sewn.
"She was subsequently free from obstacles" means:
in the absence of any obstacle.
"Nor should she sew herself" means she should not sew by herself.
"Nor should she make an effort to have it sewn" means...
One should not command another,
except for four or five days— meaning,
setting aside a period of four or five days.
“‘I will neither sew it nor make an effort to have it sewn’”— by the mere fact of relinquishing the responsibility, there is an offense of *pācittiya*.
If one who is fully ordained perceives another as fully ordained, and having had her robe unsewn or having had it unsewn for her,
she subsequently— without any obstacle— neither sews it herself nor makes an effort to have it sewn, except within four or five days, there is an offense of *pācittiya*.

If one who is fully ordained, being in doubt, has unsewn or caused to be unsewn a robe, and subsequently, when there is no obstacle, neither sews it herself nor makes an effort to have it sewn— except within four or five days— there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
If one who is fully ordained, perceiving another as not fully ordained, has unsewn or caused to be unsewn a robe, and subsequently, when there is no obstacle,
neither sews it herself nor makes an effort to have it sewn— except within four or five days— [there is an offense of expiation].
There is an offense of expiation (*pācittiya*).

If, having had another requisite unsewn or having had it unsewn, she subsequently—being free from obstacles—neither sews it herself nor makes an effort to have it sewn, except for a period of four or five days, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*).
[The same applies if] she has had a robe or another requisite unsewn or had it unsewn by one who is not fully ordained (*anupasampannā*).
If afterwards she neither sews it herself nor makes an effort to have it sewn, except after four or five days, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
If [the person] is not ordained, but she perceives her as ordained, there is an offense of wrong-doing.
If [the person] is not ordained, but she is doubtful, there is an offense of wrong-doing.
If she is not fully ordained, but one perceives her as not fully ordained, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*).
There is no offense if there is an obstacle.
Having searched for it, she does not obtain it;
or, while performing the act, she exceeds four or five days;
or, she is ill.
In times of distress,
for one who is insane,
and for one who is a first-time offender.
The third training rule is concluded.
